Retro Home-On-Wheels: A 1971 Ford Econoline “Shasta Motorhome”

CA
By Chloe Adams Car Culture & Restomod Editor • via Silodrome Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Silodrome Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • This is a 1971 Ford Econoline that was converted into a motorhome in-period by Shasta Trailers in California.
  • It has seating for two up front, sleeping space for up to four in the back, and it’s powered by the indomitable Ford 5.0 liter (302) V8.
  • Official reporting verified via Silodrome news desk.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • CHLOE ADAMS Car Culture & Restomod Editor

Heritage Preservation vs Modern Performance

Automotive passion is increasingly defined by the synthesis of analog soul and contemporary engineering. This coverage from Silodrome illustrates how bespoke builders, private collectors, and restomod artists are preserving the golden eras of internal combustion while adopting carbon fiber composites and precision craftsmanship.

Big Picture: Auction hammer prices and enthusiast demand indicate sustained historical appreciation for rare, analog driver's vehicles.

This is a 1971 Ford Econoline that was converted into a motorhome in-period by Shasta Trailers in California. It has seating for two up front, sleeping space for up to four in the back, and it’s powered by the indomitable Ford 5.0 liter (302) V8.

📌 The Core Development

The accommodation in the rear includes a dinette set that converts into a double bed when required, it also has a space for a double bed above the cab. The kitchenette has a sink with running water, a three-burner stove top, an oven, a refrigerator/freezer, and a water heater. There is also a separate bathroom with a toilet.

Ford unveiled the Econoline van in September of 1960 as a 1961 model, and amazingly, the vans remained in production over four generations until 2014, the cutaway and stripped-chassis versions that sit under ambulances, shuttle buses, and Class C motorhomes are still being built however. A remarkable 65 years of continuous production.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

Ford unveiled the Econoline van in September of 1960 as a 1961 model, and amazingly, the vans remained in production over four generations until 2014. Image courtesy of Ford.

Volkswagen started a van-arms race of sorts among the larger US manufacturers. The VW Type 2 van sold surprisingly well in the United States in the late 1950s, and Detroit certainly noticed.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

The Chevrolet team even went so far as to copy the air-cooled, rear-engined layout for its Corvair 95 van . Ford, which began development of their own van series in 1957, went another way entirely. The blue oval engineers took the drivetrain from its new Falcon compact car, built a unit-construction van body around it on a 90 inch wheelbase, and put the engine under a cover between the two front seats, with the driver sitting above the front axle.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

A 144 cubic inch (2.4 liter) six was the standard engine, and it came with solid axles on leaf springs at both ends. The Econoline replaced Ford’s F-Series panel delivery series and it came as a delivery van, a station bus, and in a pickup variant.

Ford expected the pickup to be the stronger seller than it actually was, but buyers weren’t that interested in it. Of the 544,335 Econolines built in the United States through to 1967, just 52,121 were pickups, and the body style ended with the first generation. This is perhaps not all that surprising, given that Ford (and the American market overall) already had plenty of fully-fledged pickup trucks in production at the time that made more sense for cargo hauling.
